rows.source: UK CAA where you can fly
rows.verified: Open-category drone operations are divided into A1 Over People, A2 Near People and A3 Far from People sub-categories.
Flyer ID and Operator ID requirements depend on aircraft weight, class and whether the aircraft has a camera.
The remote pilot must keep the aircraft in direct sight and maintain a full view of surrounding airspace to avoid hazards and collisions.

rows.source: UK CAA where you can fly
rows.verified: Open-category flying must remain below 120 metres or 400 feet above the surface.

rows.source: UK CAA where you can fly
rows.verified: Open-category pilots must not fly over crowds, enter restricted airspace, carry dangerous goods or drop articles.

rows.source: UK CAA aerodrome flight restriction zones
rows.verified: Permission from the relevant aerodrome, heliport or spaceport is required before flying inside its Flight Restriction Zone.
Airspace restrictions may be permanent or temporary, so current restrictions must be checked before every flight.
Pilots remain responsible for safe and legal flight, including respecting privacy and responding safely to other aircraft.
Exact requirements depend on weight, class mark, camera, category, distance from people, location and current airspace restrictions.
Drone-safety evidence is aircraft-, operation-, location- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level aviation-risk probability.
Level crossings remain a priority public and passenger safety risk because they directly interface public routes with the railway.
Railway dutyholders must manage level-crossing risk through their safety management systems and reduce risk so far as reasonably practicable.
Risk assessments should be carried out by competent people who understand crossing risks, controls and user behaviour.
Closure or replacement with a bridge, underpass or alternative route should be considered first in a risk-control strategy.
Risk should be reassessed when traffic, user profiles, train services, nearby land use or evidence from incidents and near misses changes.
Reasonably practicable controls must be identified, implemented and kept under review throughout the crossing lifecycle.
Crossing layout, gates, barriers, warning lights, alarms and signs should be reviewed against changing risk profiles.
Highway users must obey traffic lights, road signs and crossing instructions, while crossing operators maintain and renew the crossing.
Risk depends on crossing type, users, traffic, train frequency and speed, visibility, behaviour, land use and control performance.
Level-crossing evidence is crossing-, user- and operating-condition-specific and is not an exact parcel-level collision probability.
